profile.name: Wari
profile.tagline: Ritual dance of Huari, Peru, blending pre-Inca and Spanish traditions.
profile.insight: In 1570, chronicler Cristóbal de Molina recorded the dance as Waritaki, marking its evolution amid Spanish cultural influence in Huari, Áncash.
profile.profile: Wari, also called Huaridanza, is a ritual dance from Huari district in Peru's Áncash region. It evolved from a pre-Inca agricultural festival dance, blending indigenous and Spanish elements. Traditionally performed by four dancers and two musicians with flute and drum, the choreography includes circular formations and rhythmic footwork. Costumes feature formal suits with floral shawls, embroidered knee pads with bells, and distinctive masks. Music is led by pinkullo flute and wanqar drum, creating a pattern typical of northern Peruvian highlands.
profile.profile_long:
Wari, also known as Huaridanza or the dance of the knights of Huari, originates from the district of Huari in Peru's Áncash department. Its roots trace back to a pre-Inca agricultural festival called pocoy mita, which celebrated the arrival of the first rains between September and October. This festival included dances dedicated to huacas and ancestors, featuring deer skull wind instruments. With Spanish colonization, the dance syncretized with Christian celebrations such as the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and the Virgin of the Rosary, aligning with the agricultural calendar. The earliest recorded name, Waritaki, appears in 1570 by chronicler Cristóbal de Molina, reflecting the dance's evolution through cultural blending.

The dance is traditionally performed by four dancers accompanied by two musicians playing the pinkullo flute and wanqar drum. In urban Huari, groups may expand to eight dancers plus a captain or guide, sometimes joined by two Pallas from another local dance troupe. The choreography unfolds in three main phases: dancers form circles while executing rhythmic steps with a strong beat on the fourth count, a light step called arrebato, and a vigorous zapateo (foot stamping) resembling a huayno escape step, which concludes the performance.

Costumes are formal and symbolic: dancers wear blue or black suits with white shirts and ties, covered by a floral shawl tied across the chest. A richly embroidered velvet sash with golden threads is worn at the waist. Two silk handkerchiefs match the shawl and adorn the jacket pockets. The head is covered with a white cloth called uma paño, sewn to the neck, leaving the face exposed but masked with a pink mesh featuring painted large eyes, eyebrows, mustache, and a small wool beard. The hat is a white toquilla straw with a raised front brim, decorated with a colored silk ribbon and an artificial flower crown mounted on wire. Knee pads embroidered with 35 to 40 bells each weigh heavily, symbolizing penitence and devotion to the Cross. White gloves and a command baton topped with a dog head and a leather whip complete the attire.

Musically, the dance is accompanied by two cajeros playing the pinkullo, a wooden flute with four holes, and the wanqar, a large eucalyptus bark drum with animal skin heads. The pinkullo is held and played with the left hand, while the wanqar is carried on the left shoulder and struck with a stick in the right hand. The musicians often craft their own instruments, requiring deep material knowledge. The music follows traditional patterns throughout the dance, except during general dances when chuscadas—a local variant of huayno—are played.

Wari is performed during the Virgin of the Rosary festivities, the Exaltation of the Cross in Huari, and occasionally during the Virgin of the Assumption festival in Chacas. Variants exist in Pomabamba province and other northern Peruvian towns, differing in choreography and musical tempo. The dance is a living tradition, embodying the syncretism of indigenous and Spanish cultures and maintaining its ritual significance tied to agricultural cycles and religious devotion.

sections.origins_and_history: Wari originates from the district of Huari in Peru's Áncash region, rooted in a pre-Inca agricultural festival called pocoy mita celebrating the first rains. It evolved through syncretism with Spanish colonial religious festivals like the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and the Virgin of the Rosary. The dance was recorded in 1570 by Cristóbal de Molina as Waritaki, reflecting its cultural transformation. Variants exist in Pomabamba and other northern towns with distinct choreography and tempo.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Traditionally performed by four dancers and two musicians, sometimes eight dancers plus a captain in urban areas. The choreography has three main moments: circular formations with rhythmic support on the fourth beat, a light step called arrebato, and a strong zapateo foot stamping ending the dance. Dancers move in circles, emphasizing rhythmic footwork and coordinated group patterns.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is played by two cajeros using the pinkullo flute and wanqar drum. The pinkullo is a wooden flute with four holes played with the left hand, made from waroma wood. The wanqar is a large eucalyptus bark drum carried on the left shoulder and struck with a stick. The music follows traditional patterns, with chuscadas played during general dances, a regional huayno variant.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear formal blue or black suits with white shirts and ties, covered by floral shawls tied across the chest. Embroidered velvet sashes with golden threads are worn at the waist. The head is covered with a white cloth called uma paño, and the face with a pink mesh mask painted with facial features. Hats are white toquilla straw with colored ribbons and artificial flower crowns. Knee pads with 35-40 bells symbolize penitence. White gloves and a command baton with a dog head and leather whip complete the attire.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed during the Virgin of the Rosary festival, the Exaltation of the Holy Cross in Huari, and occasionally the Virgin of the Assumption in Chacas. The dance marks the agricultural cycle's start of rains and reflects syncretism between indigenous and Christian traditions, embodying devotion and penitence.
sections.regional_variants: Variants exist in Pomabamba province and towns like Sihuas, Urpay, Taurija, and Pataz, differing in choreography and musical tempo from the Huari version.
sections.lineage: Descended from pre-Inca agricultural dances linked to the pocoy mita festival, evolving through Spanish colonial influence and Christian religious festivals into the current Wari dance.

profile.sacred_note: Wari is a ritual dance with penitential symbolism, performed in religious festivals and embodying devotion to the Cross; outsiders should respect its sacred context and not appropriate its masks or costumes.

music_profile.sound_description: The music features a wooden pinkullo flute with a clear, piercing tone and a large wanqar drum providing deep, resonant beats. The rhythm emphasizes the fourth beat, creating a steady, ritualistic pulse typical of northern Peruvian highlands.

claims.text: La huaridanza, también llamada danza de los caballeros de Huari, es una danza ritual de origen mestizo andino-español, originario del distrito de Huari, en el departamento peruano de Áncash.
claims.quote: La huaridanza, también llamada danza de los caballeros de Huari, es una danza ritual de origen mestizo andino-español, originario del distrito de Huari, en el departamento peruano de Áncash.

claims.text: Su origen se remonta al período del sincretismo inca y español a partir de una danza mucho más antigua, posiblemente de origen preinca.
claims.quote: Su origen se remonta al período del sincretismo inca y español a partir de una danza mucho más antigua, posiblemente de origen preinca.

claims.text: En 1570, el cronista Cristóbal de Molina detalla que la danza tenía como nombre Waritaki, esta evolucionó a medida que la nueva cultura española se consolidaba en la región.
claims.quote: En 1570, el cronista Cristóbal de Molina detalla que la danza tenía como nombre Waritaki, esta evolucionó a medida que la nueva cultura española se consolidaba en la región.

claims.text: Está compuesta tradicionalmente de cuatro danzantes y dos músicos de flauta y tambor llamados cajeros.
claims.quote: Está compuesta tradicionalmente de cuatro danzantes y dos músicos de flauta y tambor llamados cajeros.

claims.text: La coreografía de la huaridanza tiene tres 'momentos' fundamentales, en que los danzantes hacen el recorrido formando círculos, con la apoyatura rítmica en el cuarto compás, el arrebato, que es un paso ligero, y el jaleo o zapateo, con un paso fuerte a modo de fuga de huayno.

claims.text: El traje base es una vestimenta formal compuesta por un conjunto de terno azul o negro, camisa blanca y corbata, cubierto por un pañolón de tela floreada y con flecos.
claims.quote: El traje base es una vestimenta formal compuesta por un conjunto de terno azul o negro, camisa blanca y corbata. El terno es cubierto por un pañolón, de tela floreada y con flecos.

claims.text: Las rodilleras de pana, ricamente bordadas, tienen hileras de 35 a 40 cascabeles cada una, cuyo gran peso es entendido como una forma de penitencia.
claims.quote: Atadas a las rodillas lleva rodilleras de pana, ricamente bordadas, con hileras de 35 a 40 cascabeles cada una, cuyo gran peso es entendido como una forma de penitencia.

claims.text: La música es interpretada por dos músicos llamados cajeros, que portan un pinkullo, flauta de madera, y una caja o wanqar, tambor membranófono.
claims.quote: Dos músicos, conocidos como cajeros, portan un pinkullo, flauta con embocadura de pico... El otro instrumento es la caja o wanqar, membranófono hecho de corteza de eucalipto.

claims.text: Las tonadas que se interpretan siguen un patrón tradicional durante la mayor parte del desempeño de la cuadrilla; solamente en las ocasiones en que se invita a un baile general se interpretan chuscadas.
claims.quote: Las tonadas que se interpretan siguen un patrón tradicional durante la mayor parte del desempeño de la cuadrilla; solamente en las ocasiones en que se invita a un baile general se interpretan chuscadas.

claims.text: Se presentan durante las festividades de la Virgen del Rosario, patrona de la ciudad de Huari en la exaltación de la cruz del mismo pueblo y, ocasionalmente, en la fiesta de la Virgen de la Asunción de Chacas.
